definitions.definition: 'Appellate Tribunal' means the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal established under section 14 of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997.
definitions.plain_english: The Appellate Tribunal is an existing government body — the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) — that has been given the additional role of hearing appeals against orders passed by the Data Protection Board of India under this Act. If someone is unhappy with a decision made by the Board, they can challenge it before this Tribunal. It acts as the next level of legal review above the Board.
real_world_examples: A large Indian e-commerce company is penalised by the Data Protection Board for failing to implement adequate data security measures after a user data breach. The company disagrees with the penalty amount and files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) within 60 days of receiving the Board's order.

An individual Data Principal in Mumbai complaints to the Board that her personal data was misused by a fintech app, but the Board dismisses her complaint. She approaches the Appellate Tribunal to challenge the dismissal order and seek reconsideration.

A Significant Data Fiduciary operating a popular health-tracking platform in India receives a direction from the Board to delete certain unlawfully retained data. The company believes the direction is disproportionate and prefers an appeal before TDSAT to have the direction modified or set aside.

A Consent Manager registered with the Board has its registration revoked by the Board following an inquiry. The Consent Manager appeals to the Appellate Tribunal, arguing the revocation was procedurally unfair, and TDSAT proceeds to hear both parties before passing its order.

A startup in Bengaluru operating an AI-based recruitment tool is found by the Board to have processed personal data beyond the specified purpose. The startup files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal citing insufficient cause for the Board's finding, and the Tribunal entertains the appeal even after the 60-day period on showing sufficient cause.
what_it_covers: Appeals filed by any person aggrieved by an order or direction issued by the Data Protection Board of India under the DPDP Act, 2023.
The power to confirm, modify, or set aside orders made by the Board after giving parties an opportunity of being heard.
Appeals filed beyond the 60-day limitation period, where the Appellate Tribunal is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the delay.
Situations where the Appellate Tribunal records reasons in writing when an appeal cannot be disposed of within the prescribed six-month timeframe.
The sending of copies of every order passed by the Tribunal to both the Board and the parties to the appeal.
what_it_excludes: Direct complaints or first-instance grievances filed by Data Principals — these must first go to the Data Protection Board, not the Appellate Tribunal.
Criminal proceedings or matters before civil courts arising from data protection violations, which fall outside the Tribunal's appellate jurisdiction under this Act.
Appeals against orders of other regulatory bodies such as SEBI, RBI, or IRDAI even if those orders relate to personal data processing, as only Board orders under this Act are appealable here.
The Data Protection Board of India itself, which is a separate body and the original adjudicating authority whose orders are subject to appeal before this Tribunal.
Matters arising purely under the TRAI Act, 1997 in the Tribunal's original telecom-related capacity, which are distinct from its new role under the DPDP Act, 2023.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of the Appellate Tribunal determines where and how aggrieved parties must challenge Board decisions — failure to approach the correct forum within 60 days can result in an appeal being time-barred, and orders of the Board attaining finality. It also establishes the hierarchy of adjudication under the Act, with further appeals from the Tribunal lying before the Supreme Court of India.

definitions.definition: "Automated" means any digital process capable of operating automatically in response to instructions given or otherwise for the purpose of processing data.
definitions.plain_english: Automated refers to any digital system or process that can carry out tasks on its own — without needing a human to manually perform each step — by following pre-set instructions or rules. For example, a computer program that sorts, stores, or analyses data on its own is an automated process. The key idea is that the system runs by itself, digitally, to handle data.
real_world_examples: An Indian e-commerce platform like Flipkart uses algorithms that automatically process customer purchase history data to generate personalised product recommendations without human intervention at each step.

A bank in India such as SBI uses an automated credit-scoring system that processes an applicant's financial data and generates a loan eligibility decision without a human officer reviewing each individual file.
Aadhaar-based authentication systems used by UIDAI automatically process biometric or OTP data to verify identity in real time in response to a verification request from a service provider.
An HR software tool used by an Indian company automatically processes employee attendance and leave records to generate payslips and tax deduction statements at the end of each month.

A health-tech app in India, such as Practo, uses automated systems to process patient symptom data entered by users and suggest possible diagnoses or specialist referrals without manual review by a doctor for each query.

Targeted advertising platforms operating in India, such as Google Ads, automatically process users' browsing and search data to serve relevant advertisements in real time without a human selecting the ad for each user.
what_it_covers: Machine learning algorithms that automatically classify, analyse, or act on personal data in response to system triggers or user inputs.
Scheduled batch processing systems that automatically retrieve, transform, and store digital personal data at defined intervals without human initiation of each cycle.
Real-time automated pipelines such as API-driven identity verification systems that process data instantly upon receiving a request.
Robotic Process Automation (RPA) tools deployed by Indian enterprises to automatically extract, process, and transfer personal data across internal systems.
Automated profiling engines used by fintech companies to process transaction data and assign risk scores to users without manual review.
what_it_excludes: Purely manual processes where a human being reads, sorts, or enters data individually without any digital automation, such as a clerk manually filing paper-based personal records.
Non-digital or analogue processes, such as voice-based oral communication or physical inspection of documents, even if they ultimately relate to data.
Incidental or passive digital storage where data is simply saved without any active automated operation being performed on it, to the extent no processing instruction is executed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a process qualifies as 'automated' is foundational to determining whether the Act's definition of 'processing' is triggered, since processing under the DPDPA is defined as a 'wholly or partly automated operation' on digital personal data. If a process is not automated, it may fall outside the scope of the Act entirely, relieving the Data Fiduciary of obligations such as obtaining consent, implementing security safeguards, and reporting personal data breaches.

definitions.definition: 'Board' means the Data Protection Board of India established by the Central Government under section 18.
definitions.plain_english: The Board is a special government body called the Data Protection Board of India, set up by the Central Government to enforce India's digital personal data protection law. It acts as a regulator and adjudicating authority that receives complaints, investigates violations, and can impose penalties on entities that misuse personal data. Think of it as the official watchdog and dispute resolution authority for data privacy matters in India.
real_world_examples: A citizen in Mumbai whose Aadhaar-linked data was leaked by a fintech startup can file a complaint with the Board, which will then investigate the startup and potentially impose financial penalties.
A major e-commerce company like Flipkart, if found to have processed customer personal data without proper consent, can be summoned before the Board for an inquiry and ordered to pay damages.
A hospital in Chennai that fails to notify affected patients within the required timeframe after a personal data breach of medical records would be answerable to the Board under the Act.

An individual whose request to erase personal data was ignored by a social media platform can escalate the matter to the Board, which has authority to direct the platform to comply and impose penalties for non-compliance.

The Board can suo motu take cognizance of widespread data violations reported in news media, such as a telecom company selling subscriber data to third parties without consent, and initiate proceedings against it.
what_it_covers: The Data Protection Board of India as established by the Central Government under section 18 of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The authority to receive and adjudicate complaints from Data Principals regarding violations of their rights under the Act.
The power to investigate personal data breaches, conduct inquiries into Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors, and impose financial penalties.
Proceedings conducted through a digital office in online or digital mode from receipt of complaint to final disposal.
The authority to direct voluntary undertakings and issue binding directions to entities processing digital personal data.
what_it_excludes: The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), which serves as the Appellate Tribunal for appeals against Board orders but is a distinct and separate body.
Courts of law such as High Courts or the Supreme Court of India, which exercise judicial review but are not the 'Board' under this Act.
Sector-specific regulators such as SEBI, RBI, or TRAI, even if they deal with data-related matters within their own regulatory domains.
Private dispute resolution bodies or arbitral tribunals, which have no authority under the DPDP Act, 2023.
State-level data or IT authorities, as the Board is a centrally established national body with no equivalent state-level counterpart under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity is subject to the Board's jurisdiction determines whether complaints against it can be filed under the DPDP Act, 2023, and whether penalties under sections 33 and 34 can be imposed on it. The Board's findings and directions are legally binding, and failure to comply with its orders constitutes a separate ground for penalty, making identification of the Board central to enforcement of every obligation and right under the Act.

definitions.definition: The Board of Directors refers to the supreme governing body of a Significant Data Fiduciary, being the board of directors of a company or a similar governing body in the case of other legal entities, to whom the Data Protection Officer is directly responsible and accountable under the provisions of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Board of Directors is the top decision-making group of a company or organisation that oversees and guides how the business is run. Under this law, the Data Protection Officer appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary must report directly to this body, making it ultimately responsible for ensuring the organisation follows data protection rules. In non-company organisations, it means whatever equivalent governing body holds supreme authority.
real_world_examples: The Board of Directors of Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited, notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, receives periodic reports from the company's Data Protection Officer regarding compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

The Board of Directors of a major Indian e-commerce platform like Flipkart Internet Private Limited oversees the Data Protection Officer's activities and is accountable for approving data protection policies and impact assessments mandated under the Act.

In the case of a public sector bank like State Bank of India notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, its Board of Directors, constituted under the State Bank of India Act, 1955, serves as the governing body to which the Data Protection Officer reports.

A large Indian health-tech startup notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, such as a company processing sensitive medical data of millions of users, has its Board of Directors directly accountable for ensuring the Data Protection Officer has adequate authority and resources to carry out data audits and impact assessments.

A foreign company's Indian subsidiary operating as a Significant Data Fiduciary must ensure its local Board of Directors (or equivalent governing body) in India maintains direct oversight of the Data Protection Officer, even if the parent company's global board sets overarching data governance policies.
what_it_covers: The board of directors of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, that has been notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, to whom the Data Protection Officer is directly responsible.

A similar governing body of a non-corporate legal entity acting as a Significant Data Fiduciary, such as a governing council of a society, trustees of a trust, or managing committee of a cooperative, that performs the equivalent function of supreme governance.
The board of directors of a foreign company or its Indian subsidiary that has been classified as a Significant Data Fiduciary and processes personal data of Indian Data Principals.

The board of a government-owned corporate entity or public sector undertaking notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, responsible for oversight of data protection compliance through the Data Protection Officer.
what_it_excludes: Individual senior executives or management committees such as a Chief Executive Officer, Chief Technology Officer, or an Executive Committee that do not constitute the supreme governing body of the Significant Data Fiduciary.
The Data Protection Board of India constituted under this Act, which is a separate statutory body and entirely distinct from the internal Board of Directors of a Data Fiduciary.

Advisory boards, audit committees, or sub-committees of a company that may assist the Board of Directors but do not independently constitute the supreme governing authority of the Significant Data Fiduciary.

Shareholders or members of a company in general meeting, who hold ownership interests but do not form part of the governing body responsible for managing and directing the affairs of the organisation on a day-to-day and strategic basis.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity and functioning of the Board of Directors is legally significant because the Data Protection Officer of a Significant Data Fiduciary must be directly responsible to this body, ensuring top-level accountability for data protection compliance; failure to maintain this reporting structure or appointing a DPO who is not accountable to the Board of Directors may constitute non-compliance with Section 10, potentially attracting penalties under the Act.

definitions.definition: A 'body corporate' means any company or association or body of persons incorporated under any law relating to companies for the time being in force in India or in a foreign country. As used in this Act, the term encompasses entities having a distinct legal personality, capable of holding property, entering into contracts, and suing or being sued in their own name.
definitions.plain_english: A body corporate is any legally registered company or organisation that has been given its own legal identity separate from the people who own or run it. This means it can own property, sign contracts, take legal action, and be held legally responsible in its own name. In the context of Indian data protection law, companies that handle personal data of Indian users are treated as bodies corporate and can face penalties for violations.
real_world_examples: An Indian e-commerce company like Flipkart Internet Private Limited, incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, that collects and processes customer personal data is a body corporate subject to data protection obligations.

A foreign multinational corporation like Meta Platforms Inc., registered in the United States but offering services to Indian users, qualifies as a body corporate under Indian law for the purposes of accountability and penalties.

A public sector undertaking such as Life Insurance Corporation of India, incorporated under a special statute and handling policyholder personal data, is a body corporate and can be held liable for data breaches.

A non-banking financial company (NBFC) registered with the Reserve Bank of India under the Companies Act that processes loan applicants' sensitive financial data is a body corporate subject to the Act's provisions.

A healthcare aggregator startup incorporated as a private limited company under the Companies Act, 2013, that stores patient health records is a body corporate and must comply with data fiduciary obligations.
what_it_covers: Private limited companies and public limited companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 that process personal data of Indian citizens.
Foreign corporations incorporated under the laws of their home country that offer goods or services to individuals in India.
Public sector undertakings and government-owned companies incorporated under special statutes or the Companies Act that handle digital personal data.
Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 that process personal data in the course of business.
Banking companies and financial institutions incorporated under the Banking Regulation Act or Companies Act that store and process customer data.
what_it_excludes: Individual natural persons acting in a personal or private capacity, even if they incidentally process others' personal data.
Unregistered partnerships or sole proprietorships that do not have a distinct legal personality separate from their owners.
Government ministries and departments that are not incorporated as separate legal entities but function as part of the State directly.
Non-incorporated voluntary associations or informal groups that lack statutory recognition as a legal entity.

The Data Protection Board of India itself, which although constituted as a body corporate under Section 18 of this Act, functions as a regulatory authority rather than an entity governed by Section 44's amendment provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of an entity as a body corporate is significant because it determines whether that entity can be held directly liable for penalties and enforcement action under the Act, including financial penalties for data breaches and non-compliance under the amended Information Technology Act framework referenced in Section 44. If an entity does not qualify as a body corporate, the specific corporate liability provisions and corresponding obligations relating to data protection compliance may not attach to it in the same manner.

definitions.definition: The term 'breach' is not independently defined in the Act; however, as used in Section 33, it operates in the context of 'personal data breach', which means any unauthorised processing of personal data or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data, that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data.
definitions.plain_english: A 'breach' in this law refers to any incident where personal data is accessed, used, shared, or destroyed without permission, or accidentally exposed in a way that harms its secrecy, accuracy, or availability. Think of it as any event where someone's private data is mishandled — whether by hackers, careless employees, or faulty systems. It does not require malicious intent; even accidental data loss counts.
real_world_examples: A hacker gains unauthorised access to the customer database of a Bengaluru-based e-commerce company and steals names, addresses, and payment details of millions of Indian users.
An employee of a Mumbai hospital accidentally emails sensitive patient health records to the wrong recipient, exposing private medical information of hundreds of patients.
A Hyderabad-based fintech startup suffers a ransomware attack that encrypts and destroys the Aadhaar-linked KYC data of its users, making it permanently inaccessible.

definitions.definition: The term 'Central Government' is not expressly defined in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; however, as used throughout the Act, it refers to the Union Government of India, exercising executive power through the Ministry concerned, which is empowered to make rules, issue notifications, establish the Data Protection Board of India, and discharge all functions assigned to it under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Central Government refers to the national government of India — essentially the Union Cabinet and the ministries acting under it, particularly the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). It is the top authority responsible for making rules, setting up the Data Protection Board, and taking key decisions under this law. Think of it as the rule-maker and overseer of the entire digital personal data protection framework in India.
real_world_examples: MeitY issues a notification in the Official Gazette specifying the date from which the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 comes into force — this is an exercise of Central Government power under Section 1.
The Union Cabinet, acting through MeitY, establishes the Data Protection Board of India by issuing an official notification, fulfilling the Central Government's obligation under Section 18.
The Central Government notifies a major e-commerce platform like Flipkart as a 'Significant Data Fiduciary' under Section 10, triggering additional compliance obligations for that platform.
Under Section 19, the Central Government prescribes by rules the qualifications, selection process, and terms of service for Members of the Data Protection Board.

Under Section 22, the Central Government frames rules specifying the manner in which a Data Principal may exercise her rights, such as the process for raising a complaint or seeking erasure of personal data.
The Central Government issues a notification exempting certain government agencies involved in national security operations from the provisions of the Act, exercising its powers under Section 17.
what_it_covers: The Union Cabinet and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) acting in their executive capacity under this Act.
Any officer, ministry, or department of the Union Government authorised to exercise powers or discharge functions assigned by this Act, such as issuing notifications or framing rules.

The Union Government acting through a notification in the Official Gazette to designate Significant Data Fiduciaries, establish the Data Protection Board, or exempt certain entities from the Act's provisions.
The Central Government in its capacity under Section 19 to prescribe the process and criteria for appointment of Members of the Data Protection Board.
The Central Government acting under Section 22 to make rules governing the manner of exercise of rights by Data Principals and obligations of Data Fiduciaries.
what_it_excludes: State Governments of individual Indian states such as Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, or Karnataka, which have no independent authority under this Act.
Autonomous statutory bodies such as TRAI, SEBI, or RBI, even if they perform regulatory functions — they are not the Central Government for the purposes of this Act.
Local government bodies such as municipal corporations, panchayats, or district authorities, which are not vested with any powers under this Act.
Private entities or public sector undertakings, even if majority-owned by the Union Government, as they are legal persons distinct from the Central Government.
Courts or judicial tribunals, including the Appellate Tribunal, which exercise independent judicial or quasi-judicial functions separate from Central Government executive authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The Central Government is the primary rule-making and regulatory authority under the Act — virtually all structural decisions, including establishment of the Data Protection Board, designation of Significant Data Fiduciaries, and prescription of compliance rules under Sections 19 and 22, flow from its authority; failure by any entity to comply with notifications or rules issued by the Central Government can attract penalties and enforcement action under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Chairperson' means the Chairperson of the Board.
definitions.plain_english: The Chairperson is the head or chief officer of the Data Protection Board of India. This person is appointed by the Central Government and leads the Board in carrying out its functions under the Act. The Chairperson is also counted as a Member of the Board.
real_world_examples: When the Data Protection Board of India holds a hearing against a large e-commerce company for a data breach affecting millions of Indian users, it is the Chairperson who presides over or oversees the conduct of such proceedings.
If the Central Government notifies the salary structure and tenure conditions for the head of the Data Protection Board, those rules directly govern the individual holding the office of Chairperson.

When the Board issues a formal order imposing a financial penalty on a Data Fiduciary, the Chairperson, as the presiding authority of the Board, signs and authenticates such orders on behalf of the Board.

A complainant filing a grievance about misuse of her Aadhaar-linked personal data by a fintech app would have her case ultimately heard and disposed of under the authority of the Chairperson of the Board.

If the Chairperson becomes incapacitated or vacates office mid-term, the Central Government must initiate the prescribed process to appoint a new Chairperson to ensure continuity of the Board's regulatory functions.
what_it_covers: The individual appointed by the Central Government to head the Data Protection Board of India and who holds the office designated as 'Chairperson'.
The Chairperson in their capacity as a Member of the Board, since the definition of 'Member' explicitly includes the Chairperson.
The person serving in an acting or re-appointed capacity as Chairperson, given that the Act permits re-appointment after the two-year term.
what_it_excludes: Other Members of the Data Protection Board who are not designated as Chairperson, even if they have equivalent qualifications or seniority.
The Chairperson or presiding officer of the Appellate Tribunal (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal), which is a separate body under a different statute.
Any Data Protection Officer appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary under the Act, who performs a different role entirely within a private or public organisation.
Officers or staff of the Board's secretariat or support functions who assist the Board but do not hold the statutory office of Chairperson.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the Chairperson is legally significant because the Act vests specific procedural and governance powers in the Board under sections 20, 23, and 26, and the Chairperson's prescribed salary, tenure, and conditions of service cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment, protecting institutional independence. Actions taken by the Board — including imposing penalties, issuing directions, and conducting inquiries — derive their authority from the properly constituted Board led by a validly appointed Chairperson.

definitions.definition: "child" means an individual who has not completed the age of eighteen years.
definitions.plain_english: A 'child' under this law is any person who is younger than 18 years old. This classification triggers special protections for their personal data, meaning companies and apps cannot collect or use their information without getting verified permission from a parent or legal guardian. Additional safeguards prohibit tracking children's behaviour online or showing them targeted advertisements.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old student in Mumbai signs up for an ed-tech platform like BYJU'S — the platform must obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting and processing her personal data such as name, age, learning history, or device identifiers.

A gaming app popular among teenagers in Delhi uses in-app behavioural profiling to serve targeted advertisements; under the Act, this is prohibited because the users are children under 18 and such targeted advertising directed at children is explicitly banned.

A 17-year-old in Chennai attempts to register on a social media platform; the platform must verify his age and, upon identifying him as a child, seek his parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent before processing any of his personal data.

A school in Bengaluru shares student data (including attendance records and academic performance) with a third-party analytics company — since many students are under 18, the school acting as a Data Fiduciary must secure parental consent for such processing.

A healthcare app in Hyderabad collects health data from users; when a 16-year-old uses the app, the app cannot track her usage patterns or build a behavioural profile, even for improving services, without complying with the child-specific obligations under Section 9.

An e-commerce platform in Pune that allows children under 18 to browse and purchase goods must ensure it does not employ targeted advertising algorithms directed at those users, and must obtain parental consent before processing their personal data.
what_it_covers: Any individual below the age of 18 years whose personal data is being processed by a Data Fiduciary, regardless of gender or legal status.
A minor who is a person with disability and has a lawful guardian — both the child's age threshold and the guardian's role are governed by the same protective framework.

A teenager who has independently registered on a digital platform without parental involvement, triggering the obligation on the Data Fiduciary to obtain verifiable parental consent retroactively or cease processing.
Children whose personal data is processed by ed-tech platforms, gaming companies, social media services, health apps, or any other Data Fiduciary operating in India.
what_it_excludes: Any individual who has completed exactly 18 years of age or is older — they are treated as adults and the child-specific obligations under Section 9 do not apply to them.

Data Fiduciaries or classes of Data Fiduciaries that have been specifically exempted by prescribed rules under Section 9(4), for particular purposes and subject to conditions, from the parental consent and tracking prohibition requirements.

Processing by a Data Fiduciary that the Central Government has notified under Section 9(5) as verifiably safe, where a higher age threshold has been prescribed, meaning children above that notified age are excluded from the parental consent and tracking prohibition obligations for that specific Data Fiduciary.

The parents or lawful guardians themselves — while they are included within the definition of 'Data Principal' on behalf of the child, they are not themselves 'children' for the purposes of these special protections.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a data subject qualifies as a 'child' determines whether a Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable parental consent before processing personal data, and whether prohibitions on behavioural tracking and targeted advertising are triggered under Section 9; failure to comply can expose a Data Fiduciary to significant financial penalties under the Act's penalty framework. It also defines the scope of the 'Data Principal' — including parents and lawful guardians acting on the child's behalf — thereby expanding the circle of persons whose consent and rights must be respected.

definitions.definition: The term 'complaint' is not formally defined in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, but as used in sections 5 and 31, it means a formal grievance made by a Data Principal to the Data Protection Board of India against a Data Fiduciary or Data Processor alleging a violation of the rights or obligations prescribed under this Act, submitted in such manner as may be prescribed.
definitions.plain_english: A complaint is an official grievance that an individual (whose personal data is being processed) can file with the Data Protection Board of India when they believe their data privacy rights have been violated. For example, if a company misuses your personal data or refuses to delete it when asked, you can file a complaint. The complaint triggers a formal inquiry process by the Board against the responsible party.
real_world_examples: A resident of Mumbai receives unsolicited promotional messages from an e-commerce platform even after withdrawing consent for marketing communications, and files a complaint with the Data Protection Board alleging violation of her right to withdraw consent under the Act.

A student in Bengaluru discovers that an EdTech company has shared her personal data including academic records with third-party advertisers without her knowledge or consent, and lodges a complaint with the Board seeking redressal.

An employee in Delhi finds that his employer has processed his biometric and health data beyond the specified purpose communicated at the time of collection and files a complaint against the company as a Data Fiduciary.

A user of a popular Indian fintech app in Chennai notices that her data has been leaked in a personal data breach and that the company failed to notify her or the Board as required, prompting her to file a formal complaint with the Data Protection Board of India.

A parent in Hyderabad complains to the Board after discovering that a children's gaming app has collected and processed her minor child's personal data without obtaining verifiable parental consent as mandated under the Act.
what_it_covers: A complaint filed by a Data Principal against a Data Fiduciary for processing personal data beyond the specified purpose communicated in the notice.
A complaint alleging failure by a Data Fiduciary to honour a Data Principal's request for erasure or correction of personal data under section 13.
A complaint made by a Data Principal regarding a personal data breach where the Data Fiduciary failed to notify affected individuals or the Board as required.
A complaint by a Data Principal against a Consent Manager for failing to facilitate proper management or withdrawal of consent through the prescribed platform.
A complaint filed on behalf of a child or person with disability by their lawful guardian alleging violation of heightened protections under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Complaints filed by entities other than Data Principals (such as competitors or industry bodies) against a Data Fiduciary, as the complaint mechanism is specifically available to affected individuals whose personal data is at issue.

General consumer grievances unrelated to the processing of personal data, such as product defects or service quality issues not involving personal data rights, which fall outside the Board's jurisdiction.

Complaints that have not first been addressed through the Data Fiduciary's own grievance redressal mechanism, as the Act contemplates exhaustion of available internal remedies before escalation to the Board.

Anonymous or pseudonymous submissions that cannot be traced to an identifiable Data Principal, as a complaint must come from an identifiable individual whose personal data is the subject of the alleged violation.
Appeals to the Appellate Tribunal, which are a distinct legal remedy separate from the initial complaint filed with the Board.
definitions.why_it_matters: The filing of a valid complaint activates the Data Protection Board's adjudicatory jurisdiction under section 31, enabling the Board to inquire into alleged violations, impose financial penalties on Data Fiduciaries or Data Processors under the Schedule, and grant relief to the aggrieved Data Principal. Without a properly filed complaint, the Board's enforcement machinery cannot be set in motion against a non-compliant Data Fiduciary.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 37 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, 'computer resource' shall have the meaning assigned to it in the Information Technology Act, 2000, which defines it as any computer, computer system, computer network, data, computer database or software.
definitions.plain_english: A 'computer resource' is any digital device, system, or network — such as a website, server, mobile app, cloud platform, or database — that stores, transmits, or processes information electronically. In the context of this law, it refers specifically to the digital infrastructure a business uses to offer goods or services to people in India. When a company repeatedly violates data protection rules, the government can order that the public's access to its services running on such resources be blocked.
real_world_examples: An e-commerce platform like Flipkart operating servers and databases in India or abroad that host its website and mobile application — these constitute computer resources that could be blocked if Flipkart repeatedly violates data protection obligations.

A fintech startup's cloud-based payment gateway hosted on AWS India or Azure data centres, through which it processes transactions for Indian users, qualifies as a computer resource subject to blocking directions under Section 37.

A social media company's content delivery network and backend servers that enable Indian users to access its platform — including all associated software and databases — are computer resources that the Central Government could direct intermediaries to block.

An online gaming company's game servers, user-account databases, and API infrastructure that Indian players connect to in order to play games and make in-app purchases constitute computer resources under this provision.

definitions.definition: Consent, though not separately defined in Section 2, is used throughout the Act to mean a free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous indication of the Data Principal's wishes, given by a clear affirmative action signifying agreement to the processing of her personal data, and which may be withdrawn at any time. Such consent must be given for a specified purpose and is distinct from any consent given under coercion, deception, or as a bundled condition of service unrelated to the processing in question.
definitions.plain_english: Consent means that a person has clearly and voluntarily said 'yes' to a company or organisation collecting or using their personal data for a specific reason. The person must be properly informed about what data is being collected and why before they agree. Importantly, a person can take back their consent at any point, and refusing or withdrawing consent must not put them at a disadvantage for services that do not actually require that data.
real_world_examples: A user downloading a health-tracking app in India is shown a clear notice explaining that their location and health data will be used to suggest nearby doctors; the user ticks a checkbox marked 'I agree' — this constitutes valid consent under the Act.

A bank customer in Mumbai completing a video-based KYC process on the bank's mobile app is shown a notice describing the personal data to be collected and its purpose; the customer proceeds with the process, signifying affirmative consent.

An e-commerce platform like Flipkart asks a shopper to consent to sharing their purchase history with third-party advertisers; the shopper must actively select 'Yes, I agree' rather than having the option pre-ticked for this to be valid consent.

A patient at a private hospital in Delhi consents to their medical records being shared with a specialist clinic by signing a digital form that clearly states which records will be shared and for what treatment purpose.

A job applicant on a recruitment platform is asked separately whether they consent to their resume being shared with partner companies beyond the one they applied to; clicking a dedicated 'Allow sharing' button constitutes specific, informed consent.

A parent providing consent on behalf of their minor child for an ed-tech platform to process the child's learning data must do so through a verifiable mechanism, ensuring the consent is traceable to the lawful guardian.
what_it_covers: An explicit, affirmative action by a Data Principal — such as clicking an 'I agree' button or signing a digital form — after receiving a prescribed notice describing the data and its purpose.
Consent given through a Consent Manager platform, where the Data Principal uses a registered intermediary to grant, manage, review, or withdraw consent in an accessible and interoperable manner.
Consent provided by a parent or lawful guardian on behalf of a child (under 18 years) or a person with disability, acting as the Data Principal for the purpose of processing personal data.
Previously given consent (before commencement of the Act) that a Data Fiduciary must seek to reaffirm in compliance with the new notice and consent requirements within prescribed timelines.
Withdrawal of consent, which is treated as a legitimate exercise of the Data Principal's right and must be honoured by the Data Fiduciary without prejudice to prior lawful processing.
what_it_excludes: Consent obtained through deception, coercion, or as an inseparable bundled condition for a service where the data processing is not necessary for that service — such consent is not valid under the Act.
Implicit or assumed consent, such as continued use of a website without an active affirmative indication — passive conduct alone does not satisfy the requirement of a 'clear affirmative action'.
Processing of personal data that falls under 'certain legitimate uses' under Section 7, which does not require consent at all and operates on a separate statutory basis entirely.
Consent given by a child directly without parental or guardian verification, as the Act requires verifiable parental consent before processing a child's personal data.
General or blanket consent for unspecified or unlimited future purposes — consent must be tied to a 'specified purpose' as communicated in the mandatory notice.
definitions.why_it_matters: Consent is one of only two lawful grounds for processing personal data under Section 4; without valid consent (or a legitimate use under Section 7), any processing is unlawful and exposes the Data Fiduciary to financial penalties by the Board under the Act. The validity, specificity, and withdrawability of consent directly determine whether a Data Fiduciary's obligations under Sections 5, 6, 8, 9, and 11 are triggered, including duties of notice, data minimisation, accuracy, and honoring withdrawal requests.

definitions.definition: "Consent Manager" means a person registered with the Board, who acts as a single point of contact to enable a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw her consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
definitions.plain_english: A Consent Manager is a registered intermediary that serves as a one-stop platform allowing individuals to control their personal data consent across multiple services. Through this platform, a person can give permission to use their data, check what they have agreed to, and take back that permission at any time. The Consent Manager must be officially registered with the Data Protection Board of India and must operate in a way that is easy to use, open about its workings, and compatible with other systems.
real_world_examples: A fintech aggregator platform in India registers as a Consent Manager with the Board and offers a unified dashboard where users can grant, view, and revoke consent for sharing their financial data across multiple banks and NBFCs under the Account Aggregator framework.

A health-tech company in Bengaluru registers as a Consent Manager to allow patients to manage consent for sharing their electronic health records across hospitals, diagnostic labs, and insurance providers under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission.

A large telecom operator in India registers as a Consent Manager, enabling its subscribers to control which third-party apps and advertisers may access their usage data, demographic information, and location data through a single mobile application interface.

A government-approved Consent Manager platform in Mumbai provides rural citizens with a simple, multilingual interface to grant or withdraw consent for their agricultural land records and Aadhaar-linked data being shared with banks for crop loan processing.

An ed-tech aggregator registers as a Consent Manager so that students and parents can use one portal to manage consents given to various online learning platforms, examination bodies, and scholarship portals that process their personal data.
what_it_covers: A fintech or health-tech entity that is formally registered with the Data Protection Board of India and operates a platform enabling users to give, manage, review, and withdraw data processing consents.

Any person (including a company or body corporate) that provides a technologically accessible, transparent, and interoperable interface acting as the single point of contact for consent management on behalf of Data Principals.

An entity that facilitates consent flows between Data Principals and multiple Data Fiduciaries by providing a unified, standardised dashboard or application through which all consent-related actions can be performed.

Entities operating under frameworks such as India's Account Aggregator or Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission that perform the functional role of aggregating and managing user consents across multiple service providers.
what_it_excludes: A Data Fiduciary that collects and manages consent only for its own data processing operations and does not act as a third-party intermediary or single point of contact for consent across multiple entities.

An unregistered person or platform that facilitates consent-related functions without having obtained registration from the Data Protection Board of India, as registration is a mandatory prerequisite.
A Data Processor that merely processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary but does not independently enable Data Principals to give, manage, review, or withdraw consent.
Technology vendors or software developers who build consent management tools or software but do not themselves operate the platform as a registered single point of contact for Data Principals.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of an entity as a Consent Manager triggers specific obligations under Sections 6 and 13 of the Act, including accountability for ensuring that consent obtained through its platform is free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous, and that Data Principals can effectively exercise their rights to withdraw consent. Under Section 27, Consent Managers are subject to the Board's inquiry and penalty jurisdiction, and under Section 40, the Central Government may prescribe registration conditions, standards of interoperability, and compliance requirements specifically applicable to Consent Managers.

definitions.definition: The term 'cyber incident' is not formally defined in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, but is used in the context of Section 11(2) to refer to any act or event involving a computer resource that threatens or compromises the security, integrity, confidentiality, or availability of digital systems, networks, or data, necessitating investigation, prevention, or detection by authorised authorities. It is to be understood in consonance with its usage under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and allied frameworks governing cybersecurity in India.
definitions.plain_english: A cyber incident is any harmful or suspicious event that happens on a computer system or digital network — such as a hacking attempt, ransomware attack, or data theft — that threatens digital security. In the context of this law, it refers to events serious enough that government authorities may need to investigate them. When such an investigation is underway, certain privacy rights of individuals may be limited to help authorities respond effectively.
real_world_examples: A ransomware attack on a major Indian hospital chain encrypts patient records, prompting CERT-In to investigate; the hospital's Data Fiduciary shares patient data with the investigating agency without needing to disclose this to individual Data Principals under Section 11(2).

A coordinated distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack targets Indian banking infrastructure; law enforcement agencies request personal data from a fintech Data Fiduciary in writing to trace the perpetrators, exempting the fiduciary from disclosure obligations under Section 11(1)(b).

A state-sponsored cyber intrusion compromises the servers of an Indian e-governance portal, leading to NCIIPC requesting user data from the portal operator for forensic investigation, shielding the operator from Section 11 disclosure duties.

A large-scale phishing campaign targeting UPI users is detected by a cybersecurity agency; the agency issues a written request to a payment aggregator for transaction and identity data to identify and prosecute the perpetrators, invoking the Section 11(2) exemption.

A cybercriminal breaches the systems of an Indian insurance company and exfiltrates policyholder data; the Data Fiduciary shares personal data with another fiduciary authorised by law (e.g., IRDAI's investigation unit) for detection and investigation of the cyber incident, without informing affected Data Principals.
what_it_covers: Ransomware attacks on critical digital infrastructure such as hospitals, banks, or government portals that require forensic investigation by authorised agencies.
Unauthorised intrusions, hacking, or data exfiltration events on computer resources of Data Fiduciaries that prompt law enforcement or cybersecurity bodies to request personal data.
Coordinated phishing, DDoS, or malware campaigns targeting Indian users or entities where detection and prosecution require sharing of personal data between authorised Data Fiduciaries.
State-sponsored or organised cybercriminal activities compromising networks that necessitate inter-agency sharing of personal data for investigation under a written request.
what_it_excludes: Routine software bugs, system errors, or accidental data corruption that do not involve malicious intent or a threat to digital security — these do not constitute a cyber incident.
Physical theft of hardware or paper documents containing personal data, which does not involve a computer resource compromise and falls outside the scope of a cyber incident.

Internal administrative misuse of data by employees acting within authorised access limits, which may constitute a personal data breach but not necessarily a cyber incident triggering the Section 11(2) exemption.
Civil disputes or contractual disagreements between Data Fiduciaries and Data Principals that do not involve any compromise of digital systems or security.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an event qualifies as a 'cyber incident' under Section 11(2) determines whether a Data Fiduciary is exempted from its obligation to disclose to a Data Principal the identities of other Data Fiduciaries or Processors with whom personal data has been shared; if the sharing is for prevention, detection, or investigation of a cyber incident pursuant to a written request from an authorised body, the fiduciary is relieved of that disclosure duty. Misclassifying an event as a cyber incident to avoid transparency obligations could expose a Data Fiduciary to regulatory liability under the Act.

definitions.definition: A data audit is an independent evaluation carried out by an independent data auditor appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary to assess and verify the compliance of such Significant Data Fiduciary with the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, including its obligations relating to the processing of digital personal data and the rights of Data Principals.
definitions.plain_english: A data audit is a formal check-up conducted by an outside, independent expert to see whether a large or high-risk company that handles people's personal data is following all the rules set out in India's data protection law. Think of it like a financial audit, but instead of checking accounts, it checks whether the company is treating people's personal data properly and lawfully. The findings help ensure that powerful data-handling organisations remain accountable.
real_world_examples: A major Indian e-commerce platform like Flipkart, classified as a Significant Data Fiduciary, appoints an independent Chartered Accountant firm specialising in data governance to conduct a data audit and verify whether it is obtaining valid consent from users before processing their purchase histories and browsing behaviour.

A large Indian healthtech company storing sensitive medical records of millions of patients is notified as a Significant Data Fiduciary; it engages an independent data auditor to examine whether its data retention policies, breach notification procedures, and data minimisation practices comply with the DPDP Act, 2023.

A government-recognised social media intermediary operating in India with over 500 million users appoints an independent data auditor who reviews algorithmic processing of user data, targeted advertising practices, and grievance redressal logs to assess compliance with the Act, and submits a formal audit report to the Board of Directors.

An Indian fintech startup that has grown to process the financial and personal data of over 10 crore users is designated a Significant Data Fiduciary; its appointed independent data auditor conducts a data audit covering consent management workflows, data localisation measures, and the effectiveness of its Data Protection Impact Assessment process.

A telecom operator in India handling call records and location data of hundreds of millions of subscribers undergoes a data audit in which the independent data auditor maps all data flows, checks for lawful purpose compliance, and evaluates whether Data Principals can effectively exercise their rights under the Act.
what_it_covers: Evaluation of whether a Significant Data Fiduciary has obtained valid and lawful consent from Data Principals before processing their personal data.
Assessment of the Significant Data Fiduciary's compliance with obligations such as data minimisation, purpose limitation, storage limitation, and breach notification as prescribed under the Act.

Review of the effectiveness and completeness of the grievance redressal mechanism, Data Protection Impact Assessments, and other prescribed data protection measures implemented by the Significant Data Fiduciary.
Verification that the Significant Data Fiduciary's data processing activities do not violate the rights of Data Principals, including rights of access, correction, erasure, and grievance redressal.
Examination of contracts and arrangements between the Significant Data Fiduciary and Data Processors to ensure downstream processing also aligns with the Act's requirements.
what_it_excludes: Routine internal compliance reviews or self-assessments conducted by the Significant Data Fiduciary's own employees, which do not qualify as an independent data audit under the Act.

Data audits of ordinary Data Fiduciaries that have not been notified as Significant Data Fiduciaries by the Central Government, as the obligation to appoint an independent data auditor applies exclusively to Significant Data Fiduciaries.
Financial or statutory audits conducted under the Companies Act, 2013 or Income Tax Act, 1961, which assess financial records rather than personal data processing compliance.
Cybersecurity audits mandated under the Information Technology Act, 2000 or CERT-In guidelines, which focus on system security posture rather than data protection compliance under the DPDP Act.
Assessments carried out by the Data Protection Board of India during its own inquiry or investigation proceedings, which are regulatory actions and not a data audit as contemplated under Section 10.
definitions.why_it_matters: A Significant Data Fiduciary that fails to appoint an independent data auditor to carry out a data audit breaches its statutory obligations under Section 10 of the DPDP Act, 2023, exposing it to financial penalties imposed by the Data Protection Board of India. The data audit is a prerequisite accountability mechanism that directly determines whether the Significant Data Fiduciary can demonstrate ongoing compliance with the Act, and its absence or inadequacy can trigger regulatory inquiry, enforcement action, and reputational consequences.

An HR software company like Darwinbox that processes employee personal data on behalf of multiple client organisations — if it independently decides the purpose and means of processing (rather than merely following client instructions), it may itself qualify as a Data Fiduciary rather than a Data Processor.

An edtech platform like BYJU'S that collects student personal data including age, learning progress, and guardian details to personalise learning content and communicate with parents — it determines the purpose and means, qualifying as a Data Fiduciary subject to additional obligations regarding children's data.

Two or more persons or entities acting jointly to determine the purpose and means of processing personal data, making them joint Data Fiduciaries.

A Significant Data Fiduciary — a subset of Data Fiduciaries notified by the Central Government — which carries additional obligations such as appointing a Data Protection Officer and conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments.
Any person (as broadly defined in the Act to include individuals, HUFs, companies, firms, associations, and artificial juristic persons) who makes the key decisions about personal data processing.

An entity that only handles anonymised or non-personal data, since the definition is anchored to the processing of personal data.

definitions.definition: "Data Principal" means the individual to whom the personal data relates and where such individual is— a child, includes the parents or lawful guardian of such a child; a person with disability, includes her lawful guardian, acting on her behalf.
definitions.plain_english: A Data Principal is the real person whose personal information is being collected or used. If that person is a minor (under 18) or has a disability, then their parent or legal guardian also steps into their shoes and can exercise rights on their behalf. Essentially, it is the individual at the centre of any data collection activity — the one whose privacy is being protected by this law.
real_world_examples: Priya, a 32-year-old resident of Mumbai, signs up on a food delivery app and provides her name, phone number, and address. Priya is the Data Principal whose personal data the app collects and processes.

Arjun, a 14-year-old student in Chennai, registers on an online tutoring platform. Since he is a child, his mother, as his lawful guardian, is treated as the Data Principal and must give verifiable consent before his data can be processed.

Ramesh, a person with a visual impairment certified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, uses a government welfare portal in Bengaluru. His appointed legal guardian acts as the Data Principal on his behalf when consenting to data processing.

A bank customer in Delhi submits her Aadhaar and PAN details for a KYC process. The customer is the Data Principal and retains rights such as the right to access, correct, or erase her data held by the bank.

An employee at an IT company in Hyderabad whose payroll and attendance data is stored in an HR management system is the Data Principal with respect to that employment data, and the employer (Data Fiduciary) must honour her rights under the Act.
what_it_covers: Any adult Indian individual whose personal data is collected, stored, or processed by a Data Fiduciary, such as a user of an e-commerce platform providing their contact and payment details.
A child (below 18 years) whose parents or lawful guardian are deemed the Data Principal and must provide verifiable parental consent before the child's data is processed.
A person with a disability whose appointed lawful guardian acts as the Data Principal on their behalf, exercising rights such as giving or withdrawing consent.
An individual whose personal data is processed outside India in connection with goods or services offered to them within India, such as a user of a foreign streaming service accessible in India.
Foreign nationals physically present in India whose digital personal data is collected within Indian territory in digital form or digitised subsequently.
what_it_excludes: Legal entities such as companies, firms, or associations of persons — only natural individuals qualify as a Data Principal; corporate data is not covered.
A Data Fiduciary or Data Processor acting in their institutional capacity — they determine or execute the processing of data but are not the subject of the data protection rights under this role.
An individual who has voluntarily made their own personal data publicly available, to the extent that such data falls under the exclusion in Section 3, removing it from the Act's protections.

Personal data processed by an individual purely for personal or domestic purposes, such as a person maintaining a private contact list on their phone — no Data Principal rights or obligations are triggered in that context.
Deceased individuals — the Act applies to identifiable living individuals, and there is no express provision extending Data Principal rights posthumously.
definitions.why_it_matters: The entire framework of rights (notice, consent, correction, erasure, grievance redressal) and corresponding obligations on Data Fiduciaries under the Act are triggered only where a Data Principal exists; if an entity does not qualify as a Data Principal, none of the consent requirements, data localisation duties, or penalty provisions under Section 66 (financial penalties up to ₹250 crore) apply in their favour. Correctly identifying the Data Principal — including guardians for children and persons with disability — determines who has legal standing to give consent, file complaints before the Data Protection Board, and seek remedies.

Why it matters: Identifying who qualifies as a Data Principal is foundational because every obligation imposed on a Data Fiduciary — including obtaining consent, issuing notices, enabling rights of access, correction, and erasure, and providing grievance redressal — is owed specifically to the Data Principal; failure to honour these obligations can trigger complaints before the Data Protection Board, monetary penalties, and enforcement action under the Act. Sections 14 and 15 specifically vest additional rights (such as the right to nominate another person and rights exercisable upon the Data Principal's death or incapacity) only in favour of the Data Principal, making correct identification of this party essential to determining who may lawfully exercise or waive those rights.

definitions.definition: "Data Processor" means any person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.
definitions.plain_english: A Data Processor is any individual, company, or organisation that handles or works with personal data, but does so under instructions from a Data Fiduciary — not on their own account. They do not decide why the data is collected or what it is used for; they only carry out the actual processing tasks as directed. Think of them as a service provider who touches your personal data on behalf of the entity that originally collected it.
real_world_examples: A cloud computing company like Amazon Web Services India or Microsoft Azure India that stores and manages customer data on behalf of an Indian e-commerce platform such as Flipkart, which is the Data Fiduciary.

A third-party payroll processing firm like ADP India that processes employee salary, tax, and personal information on behalf of a corporate employer (the Data Fiduciary) without independently deciding how the data is used.
An SMS/OTP delivery service provider such as Kaleyra or Tanla Platforms that processes phone numbers and message content on behalf of a bank or fintech app to send transactional alerts to customers.

A data analytics or business intelligence company hired by a large Indian hospital chain to analyse patient records and generate health trend reports, where the hospital retains control over the purpose of processing.
A background verification company like AuthBridge or SpringVerify that processes applicant personal data on behalf of a recruiting company to conduct pre-employment checks.
A customer support outsourcing firm (BPO) such as Concentrix India processing customer personal data on behalf of a telecom operator like Airtel to resolve complaints and queries.
what_it_covers: Cloud service providers (e.g., AWS India, Google Cloud India) that store or compute personal data under contract with a Data Fiduciary.
Third-party analytics or marketing firms that process customer personal data strictly as per the instructions of the Data Fiduciary who engaged them.
Payroll and HR service companies that handle employee personal data on behalf of an employer-organisation acting as the Data Fiduciary.
BPO and customer support centres that access and process personal data of end users on behalf of the principal business entity.
Any automated software system or platform operated by a separate legal person that carries out processing operations directed by a Data Fiduciary.
what_it_excludes: A Data Fiduciary itself, which determines the purpose and means of processing and is governed by a separate, more extensive set of obligations under the Act.
An employee of the Data Fiduciary acting within the scope of their employment, as they act as part of the Fiduciary's own organisation rather than as an independent person processing on its behalf.
A Consent Manager, which is a separately defined role under the Act focused on enabling Data Principals to manage consent, not on processing underlying personal data on behalf of a Fiduciary.
The Data Principal herself, since the Act explicitly defines her as the individual to whom the personal data relates, not a processor of it.
An individual or entity that independently determines the purpose of processing personal data — such an entity would qualify as a Data Fiduciary, not a Data Processor.
definitions.why_it_matters: A Data Processor is subject to obligations under Section 8 of the Act, including maintaining appropriate security safeguards and notifying the Data Fiduciary of any personal data breach, but bears less direct liability to the Data Principal than the Data Fiduciary does. Misidentifying an entity as a Data Processor when it actually determines the purpose of processing could shield a true Data Fiduciary from its statutory duties, including obtaining valid consent, honouring Data Principal rights, and facing penalties under the Act.

definitions.definition: 'Board' means the Data Protection Board of India established by the Central Government under section 18. The Board is a statutory body constituted to perform functions and exercise powers assigned to it under this Act, including adjudicating complaints, inquiring into personal data breaches, and imposing financial penalties.
definitions.plain_english: The Data Protection Board of India is a government-established body that acts as the main enforcement and adjudication authority under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It investigates complaints from individuals whose personal data rights have been violated, examines data breaches reported by companies, and can impose fines on those who break the law. Think of it as a specialised tribunal dedicated to protecting your digital personal data rights in India.
real_world_examples: A citizen in Mumbai receives unsolicited marketing calls after their phone number was shared without consent by a fintech app; they file a complaint with the Data Protection Board, which then investigates the app and imposes a financial penalty if a violation is found.

A major Indian e-commerce platform like Flipkart suffers a data breach exposing millions of customers' personal data; the Board initiates an inquiry into whether adequate security safeguards were in place and whether the breach was reported within the prescribed time.

A healthcare startup in Bengaluru processes sensitive patient data without obtaining valid consent; the Board takes cognisance of a complaint, conducts proceedings, and issues directions ordering the startup to cease unlawful processing and pay a monetary penalty.

A school in Delhi collects biometric data of children for attendance without parental consent; a parent files a complaint before the Data Protection Board, which examines whether the school violated obligations related to processing children's personal data.

A Consent Manager registered under the Act is found to be mismanaging user consent preferences; the Board, upon receiving a reference or complaint, initiates an inquiry and can recommend cancellation of its registration along with imposing penalties.
what_it_covers: The Data Protection Board of India as established by the Central Government under section 18 of the Act, including its Chairperson and Members appointed in the prescribed manner.

All adjudicatory and enforcement functions assigned to the Board under the Act, such as hearing complaints from Data Principals, initiating inquiries into personal data breaches reported by Data Fiduciaries, and imposing financial penalties for contraventions.
Proceedings conducted by the Board through its digital office, including receipt of intimations, complaints, and appeals handled entirely in online or digital mode.
The Board's power to accept voluntary undertakings from Data Fiduciaries or Data Processors and to issue directions or orders to ensure compliance with the Act.
what_it_excludes: The Appellate Tribunal (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal), which is a separate body that hears appeals against orders passed by the Board and is not part of the Board itself.

Sector-specific regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India, SEBI, or TRAI, which exercise their own regulatory jurisdiction over data-related matters within their respective domains independently of the Board.
Courts of civil or criminal jurisdiction, including High Courts and the Supreme Court of India, which are not subsumed within the definition or functions of the Data Protection Board.
Internal grievance redressal mechanisms maintained by individual Data Fiduciaries, which are separate organisational processes and do not constitute the Board or exercise its statutory powers.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a body qualifies as the Data Protection Board determines which authority has the power to adjudicate complaints, conduct inquiries into personal data breaches, and impose financial penalties under sections 28 and related provisions of the Act. Only orders and directions issued by the Board carry statutory enforceability, and appeals against such orders lie exclusively before the Appellate Tribunal, making the Board's identity legally decisive for enforcement and remedies.

definitions.definition: 'Board' means the Data Protection Board of India established by the Central Government under section 18.
definitions.plain_english: The Data Protection Board of India is a government-established regulatory body created under this law to handle complaints about violations of digital personal data rights. It works like a digital tribunal, conducting all its proceedings online. It can investigate breaches, impose penalties, and pass orders against those who misuse personal data.
real_world_examples: A resident of Mumbai files a complaint with the Data Protection Board of India after discovering that an e-commerce platform sold her personal data to third-party advertisers without her consent, and the Board initiates an inquiry against the platform.

A Delhi-based fintech startup fails to notify users of a data breach affecting lakhs of customers; the Board, upon receiving a reference, investigates the breach and levies a financial penalty on the company.

A Bengaluru user's telemedicine app waived consent-related rights in its terms of service; the Board declares that portion of the consent invalid and issues directions to the app operator to comply with the Act.

A Significant Data Fiduciary operating a social media platform in India refuses to honour a Data Principal's request to erase her personal data; she files a complaint with the Board, which adjudicates the dispute and orders the platform to comply.

The Board receives a direction from the Central Government to examine systemic data protection failures across a class of Data Fiduciaries in the healthcare sector and conducts a proceeding to assess compliance.

A Consent Manager registered with the Board is found to be misusing its interoperable platform to collect data beyond its mandate; the Board initiates a proceeding and can recommend cancellation of its registration.
what_it_covers: The statutory body established by the Central Government under section 18 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, responsible for adjudicating complaints and enforcing the Act.
A digital office that conducts all proceedings—from receipt of complaints, intimations, or references to their final disposal—entirely in online or digital mode.
The authority empowered to investigate personal data breaches, hear grievances of Data Principals, impose financial penalties on Data Fiduciaries, and issue binding directions.
The body before which a Data Principal may file a complaint after her grievance has not been redressed by a Data Fiduciary, and which can direct compliance or levy penalties.
The institution whose orders may be appealed to the Appellate Tribunal (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal) under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Courts of law, including High Courts and the Supreme Court of India, which are separate constitutional bodies and not part of the Board's structure.
The Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), which is a distinct body under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997, that hears appeals against the Board's orders.
Other sectoral regulators such as SEBI, RBI, or TRAI, which regulate data practices within their own domains independently of this Board.
The Central Government itself, which establishes and may issue directions to the Board but is not the Board and exercises separate executive functions under the Act.
Data Protection Officers appointed by Significant Data Fiduciaries, who are internal company officials and not members or agents of the Board.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and jurisdiction of the Data Protection Board of India is foundational to enforcement under the Act—only complaints filed before the Board can trigger formal inquiries, penalties (up to ₹250 crore per breach type), and binding directions against Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors. Without this body, no statutory remedy is available to a Data Principal whose rights under the Act have been violated.
